query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of a fraction of the BCC NbMoTaW alloy with HCP‐forming elements (for example, adding ~10–20 atomic% Ti and/or Zr) will induce a controlled dual-phase microstructure. This microstructure—comprising a continuous BCC matrix that retains high-temperature strength along with discrete HCP precipitates—will improve room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy that exhibits excellent high-temperature mechanical performance (up to 1600 °C) but poor ductility at room temperature and unproven experimental irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: Replace a portion of one or more of the constituent elements (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, or W) with HCP-forming elements such as Ti and/or Zr to produce a dual-phase alloy with a BCC matrix and dispersed HCP precipitates.
generation.conditions: Tests should be conducted at room temperature to assess ductility and under irradiation conditions (e.g., helium implantation up to relevant defect levels) while also ensuring mechanical stability at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of discrete HCP precipitates embedded in the continuous BCC matrix. These precipitates are expected to lower the dislocation core energy and provide additional slip systems, thereby mediating improved ductility and serving as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: By introducing HCP phases, the alloy gains additional deformation modes that lower resistance to dislocation motion (thereby enhancing room-temperature ductility) and offer local stress relief. Under irradiation, these phases may enhance defect recombination and suppress irradiation-induced amorphization, while the dominant BCC matrix maintains high-temperature yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the alloy modified with ~10–20% HCP-forming elements is expected to exhibit higher room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased plastic strain before failure), reduced defect accumulation and amorphization under irradiation, and maintained high-temperature mechanical strength near 1600 °C.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics of the unmodified equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW alloy: high high-temperature strength but poor ductility at room temperature and uncertain irradiation tolerance.
generation.boundary: The benefits are anticipated under conditions relevant to typical helium implantations (moderate irradiation doses up to levels similar to those in previous studies) and within the operational temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1600 °C. Extreme irradiation environments or long-term thermal exposures could affect phase stability.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal fraction and choice of HCP-forming elements are not precisely determined, and potential long-term phase instability or coarsening of HCP precipitates under service conditions remain uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of alloys by partially substituting ~10–20% of the elements in NbMoTaW with Ti and/or Zr, aiming to create a dual-phase microstructure. Carry out mechanical tests at room temperature and at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C), as well as irradiation experiments (e.g., helium implantation under controlled doses). High-resolution microscopy (TEM/SEM) will be used to confirm the dual-phase microstructure and to track defect evolution post-irradiation.
measurements: Room-temperature ductility (compressive/tensile plastic strain before failure)
Microstructural characterization (phase identification and distribution via TEM/SEM)
Defect density and signs of amorphization after controlled irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in ductility at room temperature and improved irradiation resistance (evidenced by similar or higher defect densities and evidence of amorphization) compared with the baseline NbMoTaW, or if high-temperature strength degrades significantly, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Intrinsic factors responsible for brittle versus ductile nature of refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. Our findings demonstrate how ductility and strength can be controlled through the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in RHEAs.Subject terms: M

Microstructural Design for Improving Ductility of An Initially Brittle Refractory High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

Phase-transition assisted mechanical behavior of TiZrHfTax high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.
